Content:
The union of two sets [MATH: A] and [MATH: B,] denoted [MATH: A \cup B,] is the set of all elements belonging to either [MATH: A] or [MATH: B,] or both.

Content:
For example, consider the sets [MATH: A = \{ a,b,c \}] and [MATH: B = \{ b, d, e \}.] We can represent these sets using a Venn diagram, as follows:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/cc5d6524d94189422373c522bcc081f2]

Content:
The union [MATH: A \cup B] consists of all the elements that are in [MATH: A] or [MATH: B,] or both. To represent [MATH: A \cup B,] we will shade in all the area that is contained within either [MATH: A] or [MATH: B,] or both.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6d29d14c8be0f5c1e837a6338cac94ac]

Content:
The elements [MATH: a,b,c,d,e] are in either [MATH: A] or [MATH: B,] or both. Therefore, the union of [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] is

Content:
[MATH: A \cup B = \{ a,b,c,d,e \}.]

Content:
Although Venn diagrams can be useful to visualize unions, we do not have to draw a Venn diagram every time we wish to compute a union.

Content:
For example, let's again consider the sets [MATH: A = \{ a,b,c \}] and [MATH: B = \{ b, d, e \}.] This time, we will compute the union [MATH: A \cup B] without using a Venn diagram. We just need to find all the elements that are in either [MATH: A] or [MATH: B,] or both.

Content:
So, we will start with the elements of [MATH: A,] and then go through the elements of [MATH: B] to look for any elements that we do not already have. Remember that we are looking for elements that we do not already have in [MATH: A.]

Content:
- For the element [MATH: b \in B,] we have [MATH: b \in A. \quad \color{red}\times]
- For the element [MATH: d \in B,] we have [MATH: d \not \in A. \quad \color{green}\checkmark]
- For the element [MATH: e \in B,] we have [MATH: e \not \in A. \quad \color{green}\checkmark]

Content:
So, to get the union, we need to take the elements of [MATH: A] and also include [MATH: d] and [MATH: e.]

Content:
Therefore, the union of [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] is

Content:
[MATH: A \cup B = \{ a,b,c,d,e \}.]
